---
title: "Are Electric Cars Really Better for the Environment?"
subtitle: "On carbon, yes, after about two years of driving. But 'zero emissions' hides real damage that happens somewhere else."

date: "2026-11-17"
categories: [cars, environment, energy]

```{r setup}
source("../../R/fred.R")
source("../../R/ev_data.R")
library(plotly)
library(knitr)

comma <- function(x) formatC(round(x), format = "d", big.mark = ",")
tons  <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
years_to_break_even <- breakeven_miles / 15000
```

In our [last post](../2026-11-ev-cost/), we found that a new EV usually isn't cheaper to own than a gas car.
So the other big argument for EVs is the environment. But you've probably heard the counterargument:
**making the batteries is so dirty that EVs aren't really greener.** Is that true?

We built a simple, transparent model from government and research data you can check, and compared it with
the major lifecycle studies.

## The short answer

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Building an EV's battery creates about **`r battery_t` tons of extra CO2** before it drives a single mile. But an EV
emits so much less per mile that it **pays that back after about `r comma(round(breakeven_miles, -3))` miles**, under
two years of typical driving. Over its life, a U.S. EV produces roughly **half to two-thirds less** CO2 than a
comparable gas car.

The catch: the mining behind those batteries causes real harm, mostly far from where EVs are driven.
:::

## The crossover

Here's the whole story in one chart. The EV starts behind because of its battery. Then, every mile, the gas car
burns gasoline while the EV draws power from the grid, which on average emits much less.

```{r crossover chart}
#| fig-height: 4.5
long <- emissions %>%
  pivot_longer(c(gas, ev), names_to = "car", values_to = "tons") %>%
  mutate(car = ifelse(car == "gas", "Gas car", "Electric car"))

p <- ggplot(long, aes(miles, tons, color = car, group = car,
            text = paste0(car, " after ", comma(miles), " miles: ", tons(tons), " tons CO2"))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = breakeven_miles, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Gas car" = "#C53030", "Electric car" = "#2A9D8F")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Miles driven", y = "Total CO2 (metric tons)", color = NULL)

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") %>% layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = 1.08)) %>% config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

The dashed line is the break-even point: about **`r comma(round(breakeven_miles, -3))` miles**, or about
**`r round(years_to_break_even, 1)` years** at 15,000 miles a year. After that, every mile the EV drives puts it further ahead.

### The numbers behind it

```{r inputs table}
tribble(
  ~Input, ~Value, ~Source,
  "CO2 from burning a gallon of gas", "8,887 grams", "EPA",
  "Gas car fuel economy", paste(gas_mpg, "mpg (an efficient new car)"), "Our assumption",
  "Gas car CO2 per mile", paste(comma(gas_g_per_mile), "grams"), "Calculated",
  "EV energy use", paste(ev_kwh_per_mile, "kWh per mile, incl. charging losses"), "Typical EPA label values",
  "U.S. grid CO2", paste(grid_lb_per_kwh, "lb per kWh (2024)"), "EIA",
  "EV CO2 per mile", paste(comma(ev_g_per_mile), "grams"), "Calculated",
  "Battery size", paste(battery_kwh, "kWh"), "Our assumption (typical long-range EV)",
  "Battery manufacturing", paste(battery_kg_per_kwh, "kg CO2 per kWh"), "ICCT (U.S. estimate)",
  "Extra CO2 to build the EV", paste(battery_t, "tons"), "Calculated"
) %>% kable(align = "lll")
```

We kept this deliberately simple and, if anything, **tilted toward the gas car**: we count only gasoline burned
in the engine, not the emissions from drilling, refining, and trucking it to the station. We also left out the
rest of the car (frame, seats, glass), which takes roughly the same emissions to build either way.

### How that compares with the big studies

- The **International Council on Clean Transportation** (2021) found that a medium-size EV bought in the U.S.
  produces **60% to 68% less** greenhouse gas over its lifetime than a comparable gas car.
- The **Union of Concerned Scientists** (2022) found EVs produce about **half** the lifetime emissions, with an
  average break-even around **21,000 miles**.
- **BloombergNEF** estimated a typical U.S. EV breaks even after about **25,000 miles**, roughly two years.

Our simple model lands right in that range: about **`r round(lifetime_cut * 100)`% less** CO2 over `r comma(lifetime_miles)` miles.

## It depends on where you plug in

An EV is only as clean as the power plant charging it. On the average U.S. grid, an EV emits about
**`r comma(ev_g_per_mile)` grams of CO2 per mile**. Charged entirely from **coal** power, that jumps to about
**`r comma(coal_g_per_mile)` grams**, slightly worse than our `r gas_mpg`-mpg gas car's `r comma(gas_g_per_mile)`.

```{r grid table}
tribble(
  ~`Power source`, ~`EV grams CO2 per mile`,
  "100% coal (worst case)", comma(coal_g_per_mile),
  "Average U.S. grid (2024)", comma(ev_g_per_mile),
  "Gas car for comparison", comma(gas_g_per_mile)
) %>% kable(align = "lr")
```

No U.S. state runs on 100% coal, and the grid has gotten cleaner almost every year as coal plants close. The
Union of Concerned Scientists found that **over 90% of Americans** live where driving an average EV produces
less global warming pollution than even the most efficient gas car.

## The part "zero emissions" leaves out

Carbon isn't the only kind of environmental damage. EV batteries depend on lithium, nickel, cobalt, and
graphite, and getting them out of the ground has real costs:

- **Water.** In Chile's Atacama Desert, one of the driest places on Earth, lithium mining accounts for up to
  **65% of the region's water use**, according to a United Nations University report, competing with farms and
  local communities.
- **Human rights.** About **70% of the world's cobalt** comes from the Democratic Republic of Congo, where child
  labor in small-scale mines has been widely documented.
- **Pollution where it's processed.** Nickel mining in Indonesia has been linked to deforestation and water
  pollution, and refining battery minerals produces far more emissions than digging them up.
- **Recycling is still catching up.** Most of today's EV batteries haven't reached the end of their lives yet,
  and recovery of some materials, especially lithium, remains limited.

To be fair, gasoline has its own hidden costs, from oil spills to the pollution near refineries, and burning
it fouls the air in the cities where people actually drive. But it's honest to say that EVs don't eliminate
environmental damage. They **shrink** the climate damage a lot and **move** much of the remaining harm to mining
regions far from the people who benefit.

## The fine print

- **This is a simplified model.** Real results depend on the specific car, battery size, where the battery was
  made, how you drive, and your local grid.
- **Bigger batteries take longer to pay back.** A large electric truck or SUV with a huge battery starts further
  behind than a small EV.
- **The grid keeps changing.** Our grid figure is from 2024. A cleaner grid makes every EV mile cleaner over the
  car's life.
- **Lifecycle studies differ** in their assumptions, which is why we show several.

## The bottom line

On climate, the evidence is clear: an EV starts in the hole, climbs out in under two years of driving, and ends
up responsible for roughly half to two-thirds less carbon than a gas car. The battery argument is real but much
smaller than critics suggest. What "zero emissions" really hides is not carbon but **where** the damage happens:
in the water, mines, and refineries of the places that supply the batteries.

---

**How we did this.** Gas emissions use EPA's 8,887 grams of CO2 per gallon. Grid emissions use EIA's 2024 U.S.
average of 0.785 lb CO2 per kWh and EIA's figure for coal-fired power. Battery manufacturing uses the ICCT's U.S.
estimate of about 60 kg CO2 per kWh. Lifecycle comparisons are from the ICCT (2021), the Union of Concerned
Scientists (2022), and BloombergNEF. Mining impacts are from the United Nations University and the ICCT (2026).
